title: Defacement via File and Web Content Modification Across Platforms
shortTitle: Defacement via File and Web Content Modification Across P...
summary: This strategy detects defacement, tracked as ATT&CK T1491, by correlating changes to the files that make up a web presence, or to the content a system shows to its users, with the access that performed them. It matters because defacement is often the visible tip of a deeper compromise: the same access used to replace a home page or an internal portal banner can usually read application configuration, database credentials, and user data, and the reputational and regulatory cost lands on the organisation regardless of how the access was obtained. The telemetry that makes it detectable is file integrity monitoring on web content directories, web server access records for write methods and administrative endpoints, auditd records of writes performed by the web server account, and change tickets or deployment records that explain legitimate updates. The main failure mode is that content changes constantly through content management systems and deployment pipelines, so a rule that alerts on every write is useless and the rule must instead track files that never change, writes performed outside the deployment account, and content that contains hostile messaging.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for changes to the pages and files that make up a website or an internal portal. A defacement is when an attacker replaces that content with their own message or image. The change may be public, or it may only appear inside the company. This detection watches the folders that hold the site content and checks who wrote to them.
beginner.whyItMatters: The change is what everyone sees, so the damage to trust happens immediately. The same access that edited the page can usually reach configuration files and stored passwords. That means the visible change is often only the first part of the problem. Finding the write and the account behind it lets you close the whole path.
howItWorks: The monitoring service records the fingerprint of every file in the site folders.
When a fingerprint changes, the rule notes which file changed and when.
It compares that time with your deployment records and release schedule.
The web server log shows which requests used write methods, and from where.
The system audit log shows which account wrote the file on disk.
An alert fires when a file changes outside a deployment, from an unexpected account.
beginner.example: Think of a shop window display that is changed by the visual team every Monday. If the display changes on a Thursday at three in the morning, the contents are not the interesting part. The timing and the person doing it are what the manager wants to know.
takeaways: Defacement is often a symptom of a wider compromise, so investigate the access as well as the file.
Compare every content change with your deployment records before judging it.
Track write methods in web logs, because they point at the request that made the change.

objectives: Explain the difference between internal and external defacement and why both matter
Configure file integrity monitoring for web content and application template directories
Identify web server requests that use write methods against content paths
Correlate a content change with the deployment pipeline, content management system or account responsible
Recognise content indicators such as injected messages, unexpected scripts or deleted pages
Coordinate containment that includes restoring content and rotating exposed credentials
dataSources: File integrity monitoring events on web root, template and static content directories with file hash changes
Web server access logs recording HTTP method, request path, status code, user agent and source address
Linux auditd file write records showing the effective user and process that modified web content
Content management system or deployment pipeline audit trail listing published changes and their authors
External content monitoring or page hash comparison service results for public facing sites
logic: The detection combines a content change with the identity and method behind it: a file in a web content or template directory changes, the change is not explained by a deployment pipeline run or a content management publish action in the same window, and the write was performed by the web server account, an unexpected system account, or through an HTTP write method on a path that normally only serves reads. The fields that must be correlated are the file path and previous and new hash, the modification timestamp, the writing process and effective user, the HTTP method and request path with source address, and the deployment or ticket reference. Benign cases show writes by the deployment service account during a release window, content management authors publishing through the application interface, and cache or theme regeneration by the application itself, while defacement typically shows a bulk write across many files at once, edits to pages that have been static for months, new script content injected into a template, index files replaced or deleted, and write method requests from an address that is not part of the delivery infrastructure.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Web Content Modified Outside a Deployment
# logsource:
#   product: linux
# detection:
#   selection_write:
#     type: 'WRITE'
#     name|startswith: '/var/www/'
#   filter_deploy:
#     exe|endswith:
#       - '/git'
#       - '/rsync'
#       - '/ansible-playbook'
#   selection_http:
#     method:
#       - 'PUT'
#       - 'POST'
#       - 'DELETE'
#     request|contains:
#       - '/templates/'
#   filter_content_api:
#     request|contains: '/api/content/publish'
#   condition: (selection_write and not filter_deploy) or (selection_http and not filter_content_api)
# level: high
falsePositives: Content management systems that write generated pages and cached assets to disk when an author publishes an approved update
Deployment pipelines that switch a release directory symlink and then rewrite static assets under the web root
Application plugins or themes that regenerate template files on first request after a version upgrade
Backup or restore operations that rewrite a large number of web files from an archive during recovery testing
Security or marketing tools that inject a script tag into pages to add analytics or a consent banner across the site
tuningNotes: Baseline the web root by hash and record which files change on every release, then place the ever changing files, such as logs, caches and uploaded media, in a low severity bucket and reserve high severity for template and index files that should only change during a deployment. Allowlist the deployment accounts and the content management service account, and require that a matching deployment or publish event exists within the alert window; if none exists, escalate automatically. Add HTTP write method requests to content paths from outside your delivery networks as an independent signal, since those often precede a disk change. The coverage you lose by allowlisting the content management account is an attacker who abuses that application to publish hostile content legitimately, so also monitor changes to administrator accounts, uploads of unexpected file types, and disabled content approval settings in the application audit log.
